title: Symmetrical Drug-Related Intertriginous and Flexural Exanthema -- Continuing Education Activity
content: Symmetrical drug-related intertriginous and flexural exanthema (SDRIFE), formerly referred to as "baboon syndrome," is a distinctive cutaneous adverse drug reaction characterized by symmetric, well-demarcated erythematous eruptions that predominantly affect intertriginous and flexural regions. The eruption typically manifests hours to days following systemic exposure to a triggering agent in a previously sensitized individual. Commonly implicated drugs include β-lactam antibiotics, particularly amoxicillin, iodinated contrast media, and various systemic agents such as antihypertensives, antifungals, and chemotherapeutics. The pathogenesis involves a type IV delayed hypersensitivity reaction mediated by drug-specific T lymphocytes that preferentially localize to flexural regions, possibly due to local microenvironmental or immunologic factors.

title: Symmetrical Drug-Related Intertriginous and Flexural Exanthema -- Continuing Education Activity
content: Clinically, SDRIFE presents as sharply demarcated, confluent erythema involving the gluteal, axillary, and inguinal areas, often extending to the neck, perianal, and popliteal regions. Systemic symptoms and mucosal involvement are characteristically absent. Histopathologic examination demonstrates a superficial perivascular lymphocytic infiltrate with scattered eosinophils. Diagnosis is clinical, supported by a clear temporal relationship to systemic drug exposure. Patch or intradermal testing may aid in identifying the causative agent. Management requires withdrawal of the offending drug, supportive care with topical corticosteroids and emollients, and counseling on avoidance of reexposure. Prognosis is favorable, with rapid resolution following discontinuation of the trigger and a low risk of recurrence.

title: Symmetrical Drug-Related Intertriginous and Flexural Exanthema -- Introduction
content: Symmetrical drug-related intertriginous and flexural exanthema (SDRIFE) is a symmetrical erythematous eruption involving the gluteal and intertriginous regions that develops following systemic drug exposure. [1] The condition was initially described in 1984 as "baboon syndrome," named for the characteristic distribution of lesions on the buttocks and inner thighs resembling the red rump of baboons, and was associated with systemic or local exposure to contact allergens and drugs. [2] In 2004, Hausermann proposed the term "symmetrical drug-related intertriginous and flexural exanthema" to more accurately describe eruptions occurring after systemic drug administration, irrespective of prior sensitization. [3] SDRIFE is distinguished from other cutaneous drug reactions by its characteristic morphology, distribution, and absence of systemic manifestations. [4]

title: Symmetrical Drug-Related Intertriginous and Flexural Exanthema -- Etiology
content: β-lactam antibiotics, particularly amoxicillin, are the most frequently implicated agents in SDRIFE. [5] Numerous other antibiotics have been reported as triggers, including non-β-lactam agents such as pristinamycin, clindamycin, erythromycin, roxithromycin, and cotrimoxazole. [6] Additional anti-infective drugs, including nystatin, terbinafine, fluconazole, metronidazole, and valacyclovir, have also been associated with SDRIFE. [7]

title: Symmetrical Drug-Related Intertriginous and Flexural Exanthema -- Etiology
content: A wide range of other medications has been documented as potential inducers, including codeine, pseudoephedrine, cimetidine, allopurinol, heparin, hydroxyurea, oxycodone, naproxen, risperidone, ethyl loflazepate, antihypertensives, iodinated contrast media, chemotherapeutic agents, and monoclonal antibodies such as infliximab. [8] [9] Topical preparations, including bufexamac and 5-fluorouracil, have likewise been implicated.

title: Symmetrical Drug-Related Intertriginous and Flexural Exanthema -- Etiology
content: Calcineurin inhibitors such as everolimus have also been linked to SDRIFE development, in addition to infliximab. [10] [11] More recently, SDRIFE-like eruptions have been reported following administration of COVID-19 vaccines. [12]

title: Symmetrical Drug-Related Intertriginous and Flexural Exanthema -- Epidemiology
content: SDRIFE is uncommon, with a limited number of documented cases in the literature. [13] Since 1984, more than 100 cases of drug-related baboon syndrome or SDRIFE have been reported. [14] The condition may occur at any age, with reported cases ranging from 18 months to 84 years. Both sexes are affected, with a slight male predominance. [15]

title: Symmetrical Drug-Related Intertriginous and Flexural Exanthema -- Pathophysiology
content: The precise pathogenetic mechanisms of SDRIFE are incompletely understood. Current evidence suggests involvement of a type IV delayed hypersensitivity immune response. [16] Immunohistochemical studies have demonstrated infiltration by CD4+ T lymphocytes and increased expression of CD26 and P-selectin on endothelial cells and keratinocytes, promoting the recruitment of type 1 helper T cells to sites of inflammation.

title: Symmetrical Drug-Related Intertriginous and Flexural Exanthema -- Pathophysiology
content: Reports indicate that SDRIFE may involve both type IVa reactions mediated by CD4+ Th1 cells and macrophages, and type IVc reactions involving cytotoxic CD4+ and CD8+ T cells. [17] However, these mechanisms do not fully explain the occurrence of SDRIFE following 1st-time exposure to a causative drug without prior sensitization. Additional proposed mechanisms include a recall phenomenon triggered by reactivation of localized immune responses at intertriginous sites, direct drug-immunoreceptor interactions, and anatomical factors such as increased eccrine gland density and occlusion within large flexural folds.

title: Symmetrical Drug-Related Intertriginous and Flexural Exanthema -- Histopathology
content: Histopathologic findings in SDRIFE are variable and nonspecific. The most common feature is a superficial perivascular mononuclear infiltrate, occasionally accompanied by neutrophils and eosinophils. Additional reported changes include subcorneal pustule formation, vacuolar alteration, hydropic degeneration with subepidermal blistering, and scattered necrotic keratinocytes. [18]

title: Symmetrical Drug-Related Intertriginous and Flexural Exanthema -- History and Physical
content: The latency period of SDRIFE onset ranges from several hours to a few days following systemic drug exposure. Diagnosis is primarily clinical and based on the characteristic and stereotyped morphology and distribution of the eruption. Symmetric involvement of the gluteal and intertriginous regions is a defining diagnostic feature. Diagnostic criteria include exposure to a systemically administered drug with exclusion of contact allergens; sharply demarcated erythema involving the gluteal, perianal, inguinal, or perigenital areas; involvement of at least 1 intertriginous site; symmetric distribution of lesions; and absence of systemic manifestations.

title: Symmetrical Drug-Related Intertriginous and Flexural Exanthema -- History and Physical
content: Lesions are most often described as maculopapular erythema or plaques. Rare atypical presentations include pustular, papular, vesicular, or purpuric variants. Mucosal surfaces are typically spared, and facial or palmoplantar involvement is uncommon.

title: Symmetrical Drug-Related Intertriginous and Flexural Exanthema -- Evaluation
content: Diagnosis of SDRIFE is primarily clinical, based on characteristic morphology and distribution, supported by a detailed drug history and exclusion of alternative causes of cutaneous eruptions. Laboratory investigations are indicated only to rule out systemic involvement, such as cytopenias or hepatic and renal dysfunction, and are otherwise not required for confirmation. Ancillary tests, including patch testing, lymphocyte transformation testing, and drug provocation testing (DPT), may assist in identifying the causative agent, although results are inconsistent.

title: Symmetrical Drug-Related Intertriginous and Flexural Exanthema -- Evaluation
content: Patch testing, typically performed on previously affected sites, is the preferred initial diagnostic approach. Positive reactions are observed in up to 50% of patients, a limitation attributed to incomplete percutaneous absorption of the systemic agent during testing. [19] Controlled DPT is considered the diagnostic gold standard and yields positive results in most confirmed cases. Positive DPT results have been reported for SDRIFE associated with clindamycin, cimetidine, corticosteroids, terbinafine, and valacyclovir.

title: Symmetrical Drug-Related Intertriginous and Flexural Exanthema -- Treatment / Management
content: SDRIFE is a self-limiting condition, and management primarily involves discontinuation of the causative drug and supportive care. Topical or systemic corticosteroids are commonly administered to accelerate resolution, while antihistamines may be used for symptomatic relief of pruritus. [20]

title: Symmetrical Drug-Related Intertriginous and Flexural Exanthema -- Differential Diagnosis
content: The differential diagnosis of SDRIFE includes several intertriginous dermatoses, such as seborrheic dermatitis, intertrigo, allergic contact dermatitis, inverse psoriasis, granular parakeratosis, Darier disease, and Hailey-Hailey disease. These conditions must be excluded before establishing a diagnosis of drug-induced eruption.

title: Symmetrical Drug-Related Intertriginous and Flexural Exanthema -- Differential Diagnosis
content: SDRIFE may also resemble other drug reactions, including acute generalized exanthematous pustulosis, drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms (DRESS), and fixed drug eruption. Acute generalized exanthematous pustulosis and DRESS typically present with diffuse eruptions accompanied by systemic manifestations, distinguishing them from SDRIFE. Fixed drug eruption may be differentiated by its asymmetrical distribution involving acral, genital, or mucosal sites and the presence of round or oval lesions that leave residual hyperpigmentation. [21]

title: Symmetrical Drug-Related Intertriginous and Flexural Exanthema -- Prognosis
content: The prognosis of SDRIFE is excellent, with complete resolution in nearly all cases following withdrawal of the offending drug. Most eruptions resolve within 7 to 14 days, and approximately 90% of patients demonstrate substantial improvement within the 1st week after cessation. Recurrence occurs in almost all patients upon reexposure to the causative medication, emphasizing the need for strict avoidance and accurate documentation.

title: Symmetrical Drug-Related Intertriginous and Flexural Exanthema -- Prognosis
content: Systemic symptoms are exceedingly uncommon, reported in fewer than 2% of published cases, distinguishing SDRIFE from more severe drug hypersensitivity reactions. In a systematic review including over 100 patients, approximately 45% to 50% of SDRIFE cases were attributed to β-lactam antibiotics, among which amoxicillin was implicated in nearly 2/3. Other reported triggers include iodinated contrast media (10%-15%) and antihypertensive agents (5%-10%).

title: Symmetrical Drug-Related Intertriginous and Flexural Exanthema -- Prognosis
content: Supportive management with topical corticosteroids and antihistamines provides symptomatic relief in about 70% of patients, although spontaneous recovery without pharmacologic intervention is typical once the causative drug is discontinued. No long-term sequelae or mortality have been documented. Therefore, prognosis depends on early recognition and prompt drug withdrawal, whereas delayed diagnosis or inadvertent rechallenge may prolong the clinical course. Patient education and pharmacovigilance reporting are essential to prevent recurrence and improve outcomes.

title: Symmetrical Drug-Related Intertriginous and Flexural Exanthema -- Complications
content: Complications of SDRIFE are uncommon because the condition is benign and self-limiting once the causative drug is withdrawn. Unlike severe cutaneous adverse drug reactions such as DRESS or Stevens–Johnson syndrome, SDRIFE lacks systemic organ involvement and mucosal injury.

title: Symmetrical Drug-Related Intertriginous and Flexural Exanthema -- Complications
content: Secondary bacterial infection from excoriation or maceration in intertriginous areas occurs in less than 5% of cases, particularly in patients residing in warm, humid environments or living with diabetes or obesity. Persistent postinflammatory erythema may last several weeks but usually resolves without scarring or dyspigmentation. [22]

title: Symmetrical Drug-Related Intertriginous and Flexural Exanthema -- Complications
content: Rare reports describe overlapping hypersensitivity reactions, including concurrent SDRIFE and generalized maculopapular drug eruptions, suggesting a shared immunologic mechanism. Rechallenge with the offending agent provokes recurrence in nearly 100% of confirmed cases, often with greater severity or wider distribution. Psychological distress related to recurrent eruptions, though rarely examined, may affect quality of life in sensitized patients.

content: Long-term sequelae, systemic progression, or mortality have not been documented. The primary complication lies in diagnostic delay or inadvertent reexposure, underscoring the importance of meticulous documentation, patient education, and pharmacovigilance to prevent recurrence and ensure complete resolution.

title: Symmetrical Drug-Related Intertriginous and Flexural Exanthema -- Deterrence and Patient Education
content: SDRIFE is a cutaneous adverse drug reaction most frequently associated with β-lactam antibiotics, radiocontrast media, monoclonal antibodies, and various other pharmacologic agents. Given the widespread use of these drugs, clinicians should maintain a high index of suspicion for SDRIFE in patients presenting with symmetric intertriginous eruptions and promptly evaluate any suspected drug-related cutaneous reaction.

title: Symmetrical Drug-Related Intertriginous and Flexural Exanthema -- Enhancing Healthcare Team Outcomes
content: A thorough history and comprehensive physical examination are essential for the diagnosis of SDRIFE. This uncommon drug reaction is frequently misdiagnosed or overlooked unless a clear temporal relationship between drug exposure and rash onset is established, suggesting that its true incidence may be higher than currently reported.

title: Symmetrical Drug-Related Intertriginous and Flexural Exanthema -- Enhancing Healthcare Team Outcomes
content: Effective management requires an interprofessional approach involving physicians, pharmacists, and nurse practitioners. Clinicians collaborate with pharmacists to identify the offending agent, withdraw it safely, and optimize supportive therapy. Pharmacists play a key role in reviewing medications, guiding symptomatic treatment with corticosteroids or antihistamines, and preventing inadvertent rechallenge. Continuous coordination among healthcare professionals ensures accurate diagnosis, timely intervention, and improved patient outcomes.
